plan.title: At the Top of a Throw: Zero Velocity, Not Zero Acceleration
plan.story:
Maya tosses a tennis ball straight up in the school courtyard. For an instant at the top it seems to hang in the air, motionless. Her friend Leo says: "Right there, it isn't moving, so nothing is happening to it. Its acceleration must be zero." It sounds reasonable. If the ball is not moving, how can anything about its motion be changing?

To test Leo's idea we need to keep two words apart. Velocity is how fast the position is changing, and in which direction. We take upward as positive, so a rising ball has positive velocity and a falling ball has negative velocity. Acceleration is how fast the velocity is changing. It does not ask "is the ball moving?" It asks "is the velocity about to be different from what it is now?"

Now a worked example. Suppose Maya throws the ball upward at 9.8 m/s, and we ignore air resistance. Near the ground, gravity changes every falling or rising object's velocity by 9.8 m/s downward every second. We write this as an acceleration of -9.8 m/s squared (minus because it points down). Follow the velocity in steps:
At t = 0 s the velocity is +9.8 m/s.
At t = 0.5 s it is 9.8 - 9.8 x 0.5 = +4.9 m/s. The ball is still rising, but slower.
At t = 1.0 s it is 9.8 - 9.8 x 1.0 = 0 m/s. This is the top. The height there is 9.8 x 1.0 - 4.9 x 1.0 squared = 4.9 m.
At t = 1.5 s it is -4.9 m/s. The ball is falling.
At t = 2.0 s it is -9.8 m/s, back at the launch height.

Look at the change in each half second: always 4.9 m/s downward, including the half second that runs through the top. In the tenth of a second before the peak the velocity goes from +0.98 m/s to 0, and in the tenth after it goes from 0 to -0.98 m/s. The velocity passes through zero without stopping there; it keeps changing at the same steady rate.

Here is a useful check of Leo's idea. Suppose the acceleration really were zero at the top. Then the velocity would stop changing. A ball with zero velocity and zero acceleration stays at zero velocity: it would hover in mid-air forever. Balls do not do that. The very fact that the ball comes back down tells us its velocity is still changing at the top, so the acceleration there is not zero.

There is also a cause we can name. Acceleration comes from force, and the force here is the ball's weight, the pull of the Earth. Gravity does not switch off because the ball has paused. The ball has the same weight at the bottom, on the way up, at the top and on the way down, so it has the same acceleration, 9.8 m/s squared downward, the whole time.

Notice too that the same height can come with two different velocities. At t = 0.5 s and at t = 1.5 s the ball is at 3.675 m, but it moves at +4.9 m/s on the way up and -4.9 m/s on the way down. Position alone does not tell you velocity, and velocity alone does not tell you acceleration.

So the answer to the opening question is no. At the highest point the velocity is zero for one instant, but the acceleration is still 9.8 m/s squared downward. Zero velocity means "not moving right now"; zero acceleration would mean "velocity not changing", and at the top the velocity is changing from upward to downward, which is exactly what makes the ball turn around.
plan.cardDescription: Watch a ball thrown straight up: velocity shrinks, hits zero at the top and reverses, while acceleration stays 9.8 m/s² down. No air resistance.
plan.learningGoal: Explain, using the velocity readouts just before and after the peak, why the acceleration at the highest point of a vertical throw is 9.8 m/s squared downward and not zero, even though the velocity there is zero.

scene.description: Left panel: a vertical height axis labelled from 0 m (launch point, ground mark) to 5.5 m with ticks every 1 m and a dashed peak line at 4.9 m; the drawing area continues an unlabelled 2 m below the ground mark so the downward velocity arrow is never clipped near landing. A ball moves on this axis. Attached to the ball: a green velocity arrow (up positive, 0.2 m of axis per 1 m/s, so it shrinks to nothing at the peak and grows downward) and a red acceleration arrow of fixed length pointing down, offset to the other side of the ball, labelled a = -9.8 m/s². Faint ghost dots, offset sideways from the ball's path, mark the ball at t = 0.5 s and t = 1.5 s (both 3.675 m) with their own small velocity arrows, appearing once passed. Right panel: two stacked plots sharing a time axis 0 to 2.0 s (origin at launch): velocity vs time (-10 to +10 m/s, a straight falling line crossing zero at 1.0 s) and acceleration vs time (-12 to +2 m/s², a flat line at -9.8). A vertical cursor at the current time crosses both plots and the line traced so far is drawn solid. Readouts below: time, height, velocity, acceleration, velocity 0.1 s earlier and velocity 0.1 s later.

entities.label: Ball
entities.purpose: The thrown object, drawn at its current height on the height axis.

entities.label: Height axis
entities.purpose: Vertical scale in metres with origin at the launch point, a dashed peak line at 4.9 m and an unlabelled 2 m margin below the ground mark for the velocity arrow.

entities.label: Velocity arrow
entities.purpose: Green arrow on the ball, length proportional to velocity (0.2 m per 1 m/s), pointing up when rising and down when falling; vanishes at the peak.

entities.label: Acceleration arrow
entities.purpose: Red arrow on the ball, fixed length, always pointing down, showing that acceleration does not change, including at the peak.

entities.label: Same-height ghosts
entities.purpose: Ghost dots at t = 0.5 s and 1.5 s at the same height 3.675 m with opposite velocity arrows, showing same position, different velocity.

entities.label: Velocity vs time plot
entities.purpose: Straight line from +9.8 m/s to -9.8 m/s that crosses zero at 1.0 s without bending or flattening.

entities.label: Acceleration vs time plot
entities.purpose: Flat line at -9.8 m/s² over the whole flight, including through the peak instant.

entities.label: Time cursor
entities.purpose: Vertical line at the current time spanning both plots, linking them to the ball.

quantities.label: Time
quantities.meaning: Elapsed time since the ball leaves the hand.

quantities.label: Height
quantities.meaning: Height of the ball above the launch point.
quantities.reference: Zero at the launch point; up positive.
quantities.relation: h = v0 times t minus one half of g times t squared.

quantities.label: Velocity
quantities.meaning: Vertical velocity of the ball, positive upward.
quantities.relation: v = v0 minus g times t.

quantities.label: Acceleration
quantities.meaning: Rate of change of velocity, constant during the flight.

quantities.label: Velocity 0.1 s earlier
quantities.meaning: The ball's velocity 0.1 s before the current instant, computed from the velocity formula, so the learner can see the change directly.
quantities.reference: Up positive; shown as a dash when t is less than 0.1 s, before the flight began.
quantities.relation: vBefore = v0 minus g times (t minus 0.1).

quantities.label: Velocity 0.1 s later
quantities.meaning: The ball's velocity 0.1 s after the current instant, computed from the velocity formula.
quantities.reference: Up positive; shown as a dash when t is greater than 1.9 s, after the ball is back at launch height.
quantities.relation: vAfter = v0 minus g times (t plus 0.1).

quantities.label: Gravitational acceleration
quantities.meaning: Magnitude of free-fall acceleration near Earth's surface.

observations.text: At t = 1.0 s the velocity readout is 0 m/s and the green arrow vanishes, but the red arrow is unchanged and the acceleration readout still shows -9.8 m/s².

The velocity plot is one straight line through zero; at the peak the readouts show +0.98 m/s 0.1 s earlier, 0 now and -0.98 m/s 0.1 s later, so the velocity is still changing by the same amount each tenth of a second.
The acceleration plot stays flat at -9.8 m/s² for the whole flight; it has no dip to zero at 1.0 s.
At 0.5 s and 1.5 s the ball is at the same height 3.675 m but with velocities +4.9 m/s and -4.9 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Launch
checkpoints.expected: Ball at 0 m, long green arrow up (+9.8 m/s), red arrow down, acceleration -9.8 m/s², velocity 0.1 s earlier shown as a dash, velocity 0.1 s later +8.82 m/s, cursor at 0 s.

checkpoints.label: Rising, 0.5 s
checkpoints.expected: Height 3.675 m, velocity +4.9 m/s with green arrow half as long, red arrow unchanged, acceleration -9.8 m/s², velocity 0.1 s earlier +5.88 m/s and 0.1 s later +3.92 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Peak, 1.0 s
checkpoints.expected: Height 4.9 m on the dashed peak line, velocity 0 m/s and no green arrow, red arrow still down, acceleration -9.8 m/s², velocity 0.1 s earlier +0.98 m/s and 0.1 s later -0.98 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Falling, 1.5 s
checkpoints.expected: Height 3.675 m beside the sideways-offset 0.5 s ghost, velocity -4.9 m/s with green arrow pointing down, acceleration -9.8 m/s², velocity 0.1 s earlier -3.92 m/s and 0.1 s later -5.88 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Return, 2.0 s
checkpoints.expected: Ball back at 0 m, velocity -9.8 m/s with the whole green arrow visible in the margin below the ground mark, velocity 0.1 s earlier -8.82 m/s, velocity 0.1 s later shown as a dash, velocity plot a full straight line, acceleration plot flat at -9.8 throughout.

mode.initialState: Paused at t = 0 s: ball at the launch point (0 m) with a green velocity arrow of +9.8 m/s pointing up and a red acceleration arrow pointing down; both plots empty except the cursor at 0 s; readouts show 0 s, 0 m, +9.8 m/s, -9.8 m/s², a dash for velocity 0.1 s earlier and +8.82 m/s for velocity 0.1 s later.

controls.label: Play
controls.purpose: Run the flight from launch to return so the learner sees the velocity arrow shrink, vanish and reverse while the acceleration arrow stays the same; Replay restarts at 0 s.
controls.selectionReason: The answer depends on how velocity changes over time, so time must advance; this is the only transport in the catalogue for the program renderer.

controls.label: Time since launch
controls.purpose: Seek to any instant from 0 to 2.0 s, especially just before, at and after the 1.0 s peak, to compare velocity and acceleration readouts; ball, arrows, plot cursor and readouts update together.
controls.selectionReason: The peak is a single instant; playback alone passes it too quickly, so a scrubber with Launch, Rising 0.5 s, Peak, Falling 1.5 s and Back to launch height markers lets the learner stop exactly there.

assumptions: No air resistance: the only force on the ball is its weight.
Gravitational acceleration is uniform at 9.8 m/s² downward near the ground.
Upward is the positive direction; the launch point is height 0 and time 0.
The ball is treated as a point moving only vertically, launched at +9.8 m/s and caught back at launch height.
limitations: Air drag, which would make the real acceleration slightly different from 9.8 m/s² while moving, is not modelled.
The launch velocity is fixed; the scene does not let the learner vary it, though any launch speed gives the same constant acceleration.
The throw before release and the catch after landing are not shown, so the velocity 0.1 s earlier is blank in the first 0.1 s and the velocity 0.1 s later is blank in the last 0.1 s.

claims.text: With v0 = 9.8 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s², the velocity is zero at t = 1.0 s.
At 0.5 s and 1.5 s the ball is at 3.675 m with velocities +4.9 and -4.9 m/s.
Without air resistance the acceleration is -9.8 m/s² at every instant, including the peak, so velocity changes by -0.98 m/s in every 0.1 s.
The ball returns to launch height at t = 2.0 s with velocity -9.8 m/s.

carried: Check that the green velocity arrow fits inside the 2 m margin below the ground mark at 1.9 s and 2.0 s, and does not overlap the readouts or the ghost dots.
At 1.5 s, check that the ball, the 0.5 s ghost and the 1.5 s ghost stay distinguishable, given the sideways offset, and that their small velocity arrows are readable.
At the Peak checkpoint, check that the cursor, the zero crossing on the velocity plot and the flat −9.8 line on the acceleration plot all line up at 1.0 s.
